Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

This booking system manages calendars over HTTP: create, read, update, and cancel appointments.

Every booking belongs to a calendar and a time slot. The API checks the slot against existing bookings before it accepts a new one, so a client never has to poll for conflicts first. Each response returns the full booking record, including its ID, start and end times, and status, so a client can update its own state without a second request.

The API uses standard REST conventions. Send JSON in the request body, and expect JSON back. Authenticate every request with a bearer token in the Authorization header. Successful requests return 200 or 201; failures return a 4xx or 5xx status with an error object naming the field or condition that failed.

The guide has a section for each of five endpoints: listing calendars, creating a booking, retrieving a booking by ID, updating a booking's time or attendees, and canceling a booking. Each section gives the method, path, required parameters, and a sample request and response. A separate section covers rate limits and webhook events for booking changes.

Read the endpoint reference first if you already know REST APIs. Read the authentication section first if this is your first integration.

Add a paragraph on authentication.

Authenticate every request with a bearer token in the Authorization header. Request a token from your account settings and include it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Requests without a valid token return 401. Tokens are scoped to a single account and can read or write only the calendars that account owns, so a request against another account's calendar returns 403 even with a valid token.

Rewrite it for someone who has never used a REST API before.

output:
A REST API sends and receives data as text over the internet, formatted as JSON. To use this booking system, your program sends a request to a web address (an endpoint) and gets a response back, also in JSON.

Each booking belongs to a calendar and a time slot, a start time and an end time. When you ask the API to create a booking, it checks whether that slot is already taken. You do not need to check for conflicts yourself first: send the request, and the API tells you if the slot is free.

Every response includes the full booking record: its ID, start and end times, and status. Save that ID. You will need it later to look up, change, or cancel the booking.

You send requests using an HTTP method (GET to read data, POST to create it, PATCH to update it, DELETE to remove it) and a path, such as `/bookings`. A successful request returns a status code of 200 or 201. A failed one returns a 4xx or 5xx code, along with an error object naming what went wrong.

Before you can create or read bookings, you need to prove who you are. The next section, on authentication, covers how to get a token and attach it to your requests.

The guide has one section per endpoint: listing calendars, creating a booking, retrieving a booking by ID, updating a booking's time or attendees, and canceling a booking. Start with the authentication section, then work through the endpoints in that order.
